explain.say: Before software did it, engineers simplified logic by hand with a clever picture, invented by Maurice Karnaugh at Bell Labs in 1953. A Karnaugh map, or K-map, lays out a truth table so that neighbouring cells differ in only one input. Then you simply circle the 1s. Follow the chain of steps on the board.

explain.say: Look at step two. For three inputs A, B and C, the map has 2 rows for A and 4 columns for B and C. The columns go 00, 01, 11, 10, not in counting order. This is Gray code: only one bit changes between neighbours, even from the last column back round to the first. Why would that help when grouping?

explain.say: Here is a real function: F is 1 for minterms 0, 2, 4, 5 and 6. A minterm is just the row number of a 1 in the truth table. Look at the first group. Cells 0, 2, 4 and 6 sit in the four corners, and because the map wraps round, they make one loop of four. In all four, C is 0, so that loop is simply NOT C. Do you see A and B change inside it?

explain.say: Now the second loop, cells 4 and 5. Inside it A stays 1 and B stays 0, while C changes, so C drops out and the loop reads A NOT B. Cell 4 is used twice, and that is fine: loops may overlap. The zeros group just shows the cells we leave alone. Why not loop cell 5 on its own?

explain.say: Join the loops with OR: F equals NOT C or A NOT B. The raw truth table needed five three-input terms, and now you have two small ones. Fantastic! Exam tip: always check the corners and edges for wrap-round loops. Challenge: if cell 7 were also a 1, what would the simplest answer be?

draw.text: Loops of 1, 2, 4 or 8 cells: as big and as few as possible

faq.q: How do you simplify with a Karnaugh map?
faq.a: Put each 1 of the truth table in its cell, then draw loops around groups of 1, 2, 4 or 8 neighbouring 1s, as large as you can. Each loop gives one AND term made of the inputs that stay constant inside it, and you OR the terms together.
asks: How do I use a K-map?

faq.q: Why are K-map columns in Gray code order?
faq.a: Gray code order, 00, 01, 11, 10, makes neighbouring cells differ in exactly one input. That is what lets two adjacent 1s merge: the input that changes drops out.

faq.q: Can K-map groups wrap around the edges?
faq.a: Yes. The left and right edges touch, and so do the top and bottom, as if the map were drawn on a doughnut. That is why the four corner cells of a three or four input map can form one group.
asks: Do the corners of a Karnaugh map count as neighbours?

faq.a: A minterm is one row of the truth table written as an AND of all the inputs, plain or inverted. For three inputs, minterm 5 is binary 101, which is A NOT B C.
asks: What does sigma m mean in a K-map?

faq.q: Can a 1 be in more than one loop?
faq.a: Yes. Overlapping is allowed and often makes loops bigger, which gives simpler terms. Just make sure every 1 is covered and no loop includes a 0.

facts: Maurice Karnaugh introduced the map method at Bell Labs in 1953.
K-maps are practical up to about four to six inputs; bigger problems use the Quine–McCluskey method or software.
A loop of 2ᵏ cells removes k inputs from its term.

quiz.say: In a three-input K-map, a loop of four cells gives a term with how many inputs?
quiz.show: In a 3-input K-map, a loop of four cells gives a term with how many inputs?
quiz.why: A loop of 4 cells is 2 squared, so 2 inputs drop out and 1 input is left, like NOT C.

wrong.1: That is a loop of two cells, which removes only one input.
wrong.2: A single cell keeps all three inputs; bigger loops remove more.

quiz.say: In a K-map with columns 00, 01, 11, 10, which two columns are neighbours?
quiz.show: In a K-map with columns 00, 01, 11, 10, which two columns are neighbours?
quiz.why: 10 and 00 differ in one bit, and the map wraps from the last column to the first, so they are neighbours.

wrong.1: 01 and 10 differ in two bits, so they cannot merge.
wrong.2: 00 and 11 also differ in two bits.
